t_consent.overview: The front door of data protection applied to AI: individuals must know (notice) and often agree (consent/choice) to how their data is used, and each use must honor the purpose it was collected for (purpose limitation). AI strains all three — training is rarely the original purpose, and models are hungry for exactly the broad reuse purpose limitation forbids.
t_consent.exam: Scenarios probe whether repurposing data for AI training needs fresh notice/consent or a compatibility analysis, and what valid consent requires (freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous — and as easy to withdraw as to give).
key_points: Purpose limitation: data collected to deliver a service can't be silently diverted to train models — compatibility analysis or a new lawful basis is required
GDPR-valid consent is freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous — bundled or coerced consent fails
Notice must actually inform: burying AI training in page 40 of a privacy policy invites regulator and FTC attention
Consent is one lawful basis among several (contract, legitimate interests, legal obligation…) — choose deliberately and document
Secondary use is the recurring AI sin: assess compatibility, or obtain fresh consent, before repurposing

t_minimization.overview: Collect less, keep less, expose less — engineered into the system: data minimization (only what the purpose needs), privacy by design and by default (protection built in from architecture onward), and the privacy-enhancing toolbox — pseudonymization, anonymization (and its re-identification limits), differential privacy, federated learning.
t_minimization.exam: The 50-features-but-15-suffice pattern tests minimization directly. Anonymization questions hinge on quasi-identifiers enabling re-identification — 'we removed names' is never sufficient. Know the PET vocabulary at definition level.
key_points: Data minimization: adequate, relevant, limited to what's necessary — for training sets too, not just production data
Privacy by design: protection as a design requirement from the start; by default: the most protective settings ship enabled
Anonymization must survive re-identification attempts — quasi-identifier combinations (age + zip + condition) defeat naive de-identification
Pseudonymized data is still personal data under GDPR; truly anonymous data exits GDPR scope — the bar is high
PET toolbox: differential privacy (mathematical noise guarantees), federated learning (train without centralizing data), synthetic data (with fidelity/privacy tradeoffs)

t_controller.overview: The accountability core of GDPR mapped to AI: controllers decide purposes and means (and answer for compliance), processors act on instructions under mandatory Article 28 contracts, DPIAs are the required risk analysis for high-risk processing, and every processing operation needs a documented lawful basis. AI complicates each role — model vendors, fine-tuning customers, and API users can each be controller, processor, or both.
t_controller.exam: Role-identification scenarios (who is controller vs. processor in this AI supply chain?) and DPIA triggers (systematic evaluation, large-scale special categories, public monitoring). Article 28 contract contents are directly testable.
key_points: Controller determines purposes and means; processor processes on documented instructions — labels follow facts, not contracts
Article 28 DPAs must cover: instructions, confidentiality, security, sub-processors, data subject rights support, breach notice, deletion/return, audit rights
DPIA (Article 35) required for likely-high-risk processing — AI profiling and automated decisions are textbook triggers; consult the DPA if risk stays high
Lawful bases (Article 6): consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests — pick, document, and stick to it
Data subject rights reach AI: access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection, and Article 22 protections against solely automated decisions

t_sensitive.overview: The data categories with extra armor: GDPR Article 9's special categories (racial/ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, trade-union membership, genetics, biometrics for identification, health, sex life/orientation) demand an explicit condition beyond a lawful basis. AI raises the stakes by *inferring* sensitive traits from mundane data — an inference is regulated like a collection.
t_sensitive.exam: Two reliable angles: biometric data used for unique identification is special-category (face recognition scenarios), and models inferring health/orientation/politics from behavior create special-category processing the org never 'collected.'
key_points: Article 9 list: racial/ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data (for identification), health, sex life/orientation
Processing requires an Article 9(2) condition — explicit consent, employment law, vital interests, substantial public interest, etc.
AI inference of sensitive traits from ordinary data (purchases → pregnancy; typing patterns → health) is special-category processing
Biometrics are special-category only when used to uniquely identify — a photo isn't; a faceprint matched against a gallery is
Sensitive attributes in training data cut both ways: needed to *test* fairness, dangerous as *features* — governance decides, documents, and restricts

t_ip.overview: IP law meets AI at three points: inputs (training on copyrighted works, tested under US fair use and the EU text and data mining exceptions), the model itself (whether weights 'contain' works), and outputs (who owns them and whether they infringe). As of September 2026, US district courts have split on training, the Supreme Court has left the human authorship requirement intact by denying review in Thaler, UK and German courts have taken opposite views on models as copies, and the EU AI Act requires GPAI providers to adopt a copyright policy and publish a training-content summary.
t_ip.exam: Expect scenario items that turn on one fact: how the data was acquired (Bartz), whether the plaintiff proved market harm (Kadrey), whether the use built a competing substitute (Ross), where training happened (Getty), whether the model memorised works (GEMA), and whether a rightsholder opted out under DSM Article 4(3). Human authorship and Article 3 versus Article 4 are the most common recall points.
key_points: US fair use is decided case by case: training was held fair on the records in Bartz and Kadrey (June 2025) and rejected in Thomson Reuters v. Ross (February 2025); the Ross appeal, argued in the Third Circuit on 11 June 2026, is undecided
Acquisition matters: Bartz refused to excuse a central library of pirated books, and the case settled for $1.5 billion (final approval 20 July 2026)

Human authorship is required: Thaler v. Perlmutter (D.C. Cir. 2025, cert. denied 2 March 2026); prompts alone are not enough, but human selection, arrangement and edits are protectable (Copyright Office Part 2)
EU: DSM Article 3 (research organisations and heritage institutions, no opt-out) versus Article 4 (anyone, subject to machine-readable opt-outs for online content)
AI Act Article 53(1)(c)-(d): GPAI providers need a copyright policy honouring Article 4(3) opt-outs and a public training-content summary, wherever training happened and even for open-source models

Models as copies: Getty v. Stability AI (UK, November 2025) held weights that store no works are not an infringing copy; GEMA v. OpenAI (Munich, November 2025) held memorised lyrics were reproductions outside the TDM exception; both are on appeal
Trade secrets protect models, weights and prompts only while they are genuinely kept secret

t_nondiscrim.overview: Anti-discrimination law reaching algorithms: disparate treatment (intentional) vs. disparate impact (facially neutral practice, discriminatory effect) — the latter catching models that discriminate through proxy variables like zip code. Sector statutes put teeth on it: Title VII (employment), ECOA/fair lending (credit), Fair Housing Act, plus state laws and NYC's automated employment decision audit mandate.
t_nondiscrim.exam: Given a scenario (hiring model screens out older applicants; credit model penalizes certain neighborhoods), name the doctrine and statute. Disparate impact requires no intent — that's the point the exam checks.
key_points: Disparate impact: neutral-on-its-face practice with unjustified adverse effect on a protected class — intent is irrelevant
Proxy discrimination: models reconstruct protected traits from correlated features (zip code, names, shopping patterns)
Statute map: Title VII (employment), ECOA + fair lending (credit), FHA (housing), ADA (disability), ADEA (age)
Removing the protected attribute doesn't fix bias — proxies remain; fairness testing across groups does the real work
US enforcement is active: EEOC on hiring tools, CFPB on credit models, FTC on unfair algorithmic practices; NYC Local Law 144 mandates bias audits

t_consumer.overview: Consumer protection applied to AI: the FTC Act's §5 ban on unfair or deceptive practices covers overstated AI claims ('AI-powered' washing), undisclosed bots, dark patterns, and algorithms that cause substantial consumer injury. State UDAP statutes mirror it. The FTC has signaled AI is squarely in scope — including algorithmic disgorgement (deleting models built on ill-gotten data) as a remedy.
t_consumer.exam: Deception scenarios: a company claims its AI does X when it doesn't, or hides that users interact with a bot. The governance answer: substantiate claims before making them, disclose AI interactions, and keep marketing aligned with actual capabilities.
key_points: FTC Act §5: deceptive (misleading material claims) and unfair (substantial unavoidable injury) practices — no AI exemption
AI-washing — overstating what your AI does — is actionable deception; claims need substantiation before publication
The FTC has ordered algorithmic disgorgement: destroying models trained on improperly obtained data
Undisclosed chatbots, fake AI-generated reviews, and manipulative dark patterns are enforcement staples
Governance link: external communications review exists largely to keep AI claims inside §5

t_liability.overview: Who pays when AI causes harm. US law applies design defect, manufacturing defect and failure-to-warn theories through strict liability, negligence and warranty, and courts still debate when software counts as a product. The EU has settled that question: the Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853 treats software, including AI systems, as a product, eases proof through disclosure and presumptions, and must be transposed by 9 December 2026, while the fault-based AI Liability Directive proposal was withdrawn in October 2025.
t_liability.exam: Theory-matching (a flaw in every unit is a design defect, one faulty unit is a manufacturing defect, a missing limitation warning is failure to warn) plus EU currency traps: the PLD is adopted, not proposed; it applies to products placed on the market after 9 December 2026; and the AI Liability Directive is withdrawn.
key_points: Design defect: every unit carries the flaw, often shown by a feasible safer alternative (risk-utility test); manufacturing defect: a unit departs from its intended design
Failure to warn is a continuing duty: known AI limitations and misuse risks must be communicated, including after updates
PLD 2024/2853: software and AI systems are products however supplied; free and open-source software supplied outside commercial activity is excluded
PLD claimant aids: court-ordered disclosure (Article 9) and rebuttable presumptions of defect and causation, including where technical complexity makes proof excessively difficult (Article 10(4))
PLD damage now includes medically recognised psychological harm and destruction or corruption of data not used for professional purposes
Defects from software updates, or missing updates needed for safety, within the manufacturer's control cannot be excused as arising after sale (Article 11(2))
The AI Liability Directive proposal was withdrawn (OJ C/2025/5423, 6 October 2025); national fault-based tort law fills the gap

t_risktiers.overview: The EU AI Act's organizing logic: regulate by risk, not by technology. Four tiers — unacceptable risk (prohibited outright), high risk (permitted under heavy obligations, defined by Annex III use cases and regulated-product safety components), limited risk (transparency duties like disclosing chatbots and labeling deepfakes), minimal risk (unregulated bulk of AI).
t_risktiers.exam: The most reliable EU AI Act question: classify a described system into its tier, or spot the prohibited practice in a lineup. Memorize the prohibited list and representative Annex III categories — employment, credit, education, law enforcement, critical infrastructure, migration.
key_points: Prohibited: social scoring by governments, exploitative manipulation of vulnerabilities, untargeted facial-image scraping, emotion recognition in work/school, real-time remote biometric ID in public spaces (narrow law-enforcement exceptions)
High-risk route 1: safety component of products under EU harmonization law (machinery, medical devices, vehicles)
High-risk route 2: Annex III use cases — biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services/credit, law enforcement, migration, justice
Limited risk: transparency duties — tell people they're talking to AI, label synthetic/deepfake content
Minimal risk: spam filters, game AI, recommenders — no new obligations; voluntary codes encouraged
A high-risk classification triggers the full Chapter III obligations chain — that mapping is the exam's favorite follow-up

t_highrisk_req.overview: What 'high-risk' costs under the EU AI Act: providers must run a risk management system across the lifecycle, govern training data quality, produce and maintain technical documentation (Annex IV), enable logging, provide instructions for use, design for human oversight, hit accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity targets, pass conformity assessment, affix CE marking, register in the EU database, and monitor post-market. Deployers add fit-for-purpose use, oversight staffing, and in some cases fundamental rights impact assessments.
t_highrisk_req.exam: Obligation-chain questions: what must happen before a high-risk system reaches the EU market (conformity assessment → CE mark → registration), and who owes which duty (provider vs. deployer). FRIA applies to specific deployers — public bodies and certain private essential-service deployers.
key_points: Provider pre-market chain: risk management + data governance + technical documentation + conformity assessment + CE marking + EU database registration
Ongoing provider duties: logging, post-market monitoring, serious-incident reporting, corrective actions
Human oversight (Art 14): systems must be designed so competent humans can understand, supervise, interrupt, and override
Deployer duties: use per instructions, ensure input data relevance, assign trained overseers, monitor, report incidents, retain logs
Notified bodies conduct third-party conformity assessment where required; most Annex III systems allow internal-control assessment
Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA): required of public-body deployers and private deployers of certain essential-services systems before first use

t_gpai.overview: The EU AI Act's answer to foundation models: general-purpose AI models (trained on broad data, adaptable to many tasks) carry baseline duties — technical documentation, information for downstream providers, a copyright compliance policy, and a public training-content summary. Models with 'systemic risk' — presumed at training compute above 10^25 FLOPs — add model evaluations, adversarial testing, risk mitigation, serious-incident reporting, and cybersecurity protection.
t_gpai.exam: Two-tier structure is the test: all GPAI providers owe transparency/copyright duties; only systemic-risk providers owe evaluation and mitigation duties. The 10^25 FLOPs presumption and the August 2025 applicability date are precise, memorable, and tested.
key_points: GPAI definition: significant generality, capable of many distinct tasks, integrable into downstream systems
All GPAI providers: Annex XI technical documentation, Annex XII downstream information, copyright policy honoring TDM opt-outs, public training-data summary
Systemic risk presumption: cumulative training compute > 10^25 FLOPs, or Commission designation
Systemic-risk extras: state-of-the-art model evaluations, adversarial testing/red-teaming, systemic-risk mitigation, incident reporting, cybersecurity
GPAI obligations applied from August 2, 2025; pre-existing models have until August 2, 2027
The GPAI Code of Practice is the compliance-demonstration vehicle — adherence helps but isn't a safe harbor

t_enforcement.overview: Who enforces the EU AI Act and with what: the European AI Office (within the Commission) supervises GPAI and coordinates; national market surveillance authorities investigate, inspect, order corrective action, and fine within their member states; the European Artificial Intelligence Board coordinates consistency. Penalties scale by violation class, capped at €35M or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices.
t_enforcement.exam: Penalty tiers are pure memorization: 35/7 (prohibitions), 15/3 (most other obligations), 7.5/1 (misleading information to authorities) — always 'whichever is higher.' Know AI Office vs. national authority jurisdiction (GPAI vs. everything else).
key_points: European AI Office: GPAI supervision, guidance, codes of practice, coordination hub
National competent/market-surveillance authorities: investigations, documentation access, corrective orders, withdrawal/recall powers, fines
Penalty ladder: €35M/7% prohibited practices; €15M/3% high-risk and most other breaches; €7.5M/1% incorrect or misleading information
SMEs and startups: fines capped at the lower of the percentage or fixed amount — proportionality by design
Individuals can complain to market surveillance authorities; civil liability runs through national law and the modernized product liability regime

t_timeline.overview: When the EU AI Act's obligations apply, in two legal states. As enacted (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689): in force 1 Aug 2024; prohibitions and AI literacy 2 Feb 2025; GPAI rules, governance and penalties 2 Aug 2025; general application, including Annex III high-risk rules, 2 Aug 2026; Annex I product rules 2 Aug 2027. As amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 Jul 2026): Art. 50 transparency and Commission GPAI enforcement still start on 2 Aug 2026; two new prohibitions and the legacy Art. 50(2) marking deadline follow on 2 Dec 2026; national sandboxes are due by 2 Aug 2027; Annex III high-risk rules start 2 Dec 2027 and Annex I rules 2 Aug 2028. The Act reaches beyond the EU: non-EU providers are covered when their system or its output is used in the EU.
t_timeline.exam: The BOK v2.1 blueprint (approved Sept 2025) predates the Omnibus, so live items may still expect 2 Aug 2026 for high-risk rules and 2 Aug 2027 for Annex I. Read each stem's anchor ('as enacted' or 'as amended'). The unchanged dates are safe points: 2 Feb 2025 prohibitions, 2 Aug 2025 GPAI obligations, 2 Aug 2027 for legacy GPAI models.
key_points: 1 Aug 2024 entry into force; 2 Feb 2025 prohibitions (a)–(h) and AI literacy; 2 Aug 2025 GPAI obligations, governance bodies and penalties
2 Aug 2026 is still the general application date: Art. 50 transparency, and Commission GPAI enforcement including Art. 101 fines (up to 3% or €15m)
As amended: 2 Dec 2026 brings the intimate-imagery and CSAM bans and the Art. 50(2) marking deadline for generative systems already on the market
As amended: Annex III high-risk rules from 2 Dec 2027 (was 2 Aug 2026); Annex I product-embedded rules from 2 Aug 2028 (was 2 Aug 2027)
National AI regulatory sandboxes must be operational by 2 Aug 2027 (was 2 Aug 2026)
Unchanged: GPAI models placed before 2 Aug 2025 comply by 2 Aug 2027; legacy high-risk systems for public authorities by 2 Aug 2030
Extraterritorial reach: providers and deployers outside the EU are covered when the system or its output is used in the EU

t_lifecycle.overview: The documentation spine of AI governance: recording the system from conception through retirement so every later question — audit, incident, regulator, court — has an answer. The artifact set: model cards (model purpose, data, metrics, limits), datasheets for datasets, system cards for full deployments, plus training/testing records, decision logs, and version history.
t_lifecycle.exam: Artifact-matching is common: model card vs. datasheet vs. system card. The principle behind every records question: contemporaneous documentation is evidence of governance; retroactive documentation is evidence of scrambling.
key_points: Model cards: intended use, training data summary, evaluation metrics, known limitations, ethical considerations — per model
Datasheets for datasets: motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing, recommended uses — per dataset
System cards document the assembled system: components, data flows, oversight points, deployment context
Lifecycle documentation is explicitly expected by NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act's Annex IV technical documentation
Version everything: model weights, data snapshots, code, and configuration — reproducibility is the audit baseline

t_usecase.overview: Where governance starts: defining the business problem, the intended use, the affected populations, and measurable success criteria before any model is built. Use-case assessment screens proposals for feasibility, value, and risk; scope discipline keeps a system from silently expanding beyond what was assessed and approved.
t_usecase.exam: Sequencing questions: use-case definition and assessment come before data collection, model selection, or development. Scope-creep scenarios (a fraud model quietly reused for hiring) test the rule that new uses require new assessment.
key_points: Define first: problem statement, intended users and subjects, success metrics, constraints, exclusions — written down
Use-case assessment weighs value, feasibility, data availability, and risk before resources commit
Business context drives proportionality: the same technique needs different governance in marketing vs. medical triage
Scope discipline: any materially new use of an existing system re-enters assessment — approvals attach to use cases, not models
Clear success criteria enable everything downstream: validation targets, monitoring thresholds, and retirement triggers

t_impact.overview: The look-before-you-leap instruments: AI impact assessments (AIIAs) evaluating effects on individuals, groups, and society; algorithmic impact assessments for public-sector contexts; DPIAs where personal data creates GDPR duties; and the EU AI Act's fundamental rights impact assessment for certain high-risk deployers. All share a shape: describe the system, identify affected parties, assess severity and likelihood, mitigate, document, revisit.
t_impact.exam: Trigger questions (when is a DPIA vs. FRIA required?) and content questions (what does an impact assessment contain?). The governing instinct: assess before deployment, treat assessments as living documents, and let findings actually change the design.
key_points: AIIA: broad evaluation of social, ethical, legal, and operational impacts — best practice for any consequential AI
DPIA: legally required under GDPR Art 35 for likely-high-risk personal-data processing; AI profiling is a textbook trigger
FRIA: EU AI Act requirement for public-body and certain essential-service deployers of high-risk systems before first use
Common anatomy: system description → stakeholders → risks (severity × likelihood) → mitigations → residual risk decision → review cycle
Impact assessments are living documents — material changes to system, data, or context reopen them

t_datagov.overview: Managing data as a governed asset through the AI lifecycle: confirming legal authority to use each source (including secondary-use analysis), measuring quality along defined dimensions, ensuring fitness for the specific model purpose, assigning stewardship roles, and securing data through training pipelines that traditional controls don't reach.
t_datagov.exam: Scenarios test the order (rights and quality checks before training) and the dimensions (accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity). 'We had the data' never implies 'we could use it' — provenance and purpose analysis is the tested reflex.
key_points: Lawful authority first: rights to collect, rights to repurpose for training, third-party data terms, and documented provenance
Quality dimensions: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness — measured, not assumed
Fit for purpose: quality is relative to the use — clinical data quality bars differ from ad-targeting bars
Stewardship: named owners and stewards per dataset with defined accountability — data without an owner is a finding
Security across the pipeline: raw stores, feature stores, training environments, and model artifacts all inherit the data's sensitivity

t_lineage.overview: Traceability for data: provenance records where data originated (source, collection method, legal terms); lineage tracks its journey — every transformation, merge, filter, and feature-engineering step — until it reaches a model. Together they answer the audit and incident question: 'this model behaves badly — what fed it?'
t_lineage.exam: Definition-split questions (provenance = origin; lineage = journey) and application questions: lineage is what lets you trace a biased output back to a corrupted source, honor a deletion request, or prove training data was lawfully sourced.
key_points: Provenance: origin, collection method, date, legal basis/terms per source — the data's birth certificate
Lineage: the transformation chain from source through cleaning, joins, and features to training sets — the data's biography
Enables: audits, incident root-cause tracing, deletion-request compliance, reproducibility, and defensible provenance claims
Capture it automatically where possible — pipeline tooling and metadata catalogs beat retrospective archaeology
EU AI Act data-governance duties for high-risk systems effectively require lineage: origin, characteristics, and preparation must be documented

t_testing.overview: The verification battery for AI: unit and component tests, integration tests (models inside real systems), validation against requirements on held-out data, performance testing (accuracy, latency, load), security testing (poisoning, inversion, adversarial inputs), plus regression testing after every change. And the meta-lesson: passing tests reduces risk but never eliminates it — coverage gaps, benchmark gaming, and distribution shift survive green dashboards.
t_testing.exam: Match the failure to the test type that catches it, keep train/validation/test splits straight, and remember integration testing exists because a fair model inside a badly designed system still produces unfair outcomes.
key_points: Ladder: unit → integration → validation → performance → security → fairness → explainability → human-in-the-loop/scenario → UAT
Holdout discipline: train, validation, and test sets stay separate — leakage between them invalidates every metric
Security testing targets ML-specific attacks: data poisoning, model inversion, membership inference, adversarial examples, prompt injection
Regression testing after updates: improvements must not silently degrade accuracy, fairness, or safety elsewhere
Test coverage means scenarios, edge cases, and demographic slices — overall accuracy can hide subgroup failure
'It passed testing' starts the risk conversation, doesn't end it: residual risks are identified, documented, and monitored

t_bias.overview: The fairness discipline: where bias enters (unrepresentative or historically skewed data, proxy features, labeling choices, feedback loops), how it's measured (demographic parity, equalized odds, equal opportunity, predictive parity, disparate-impact ratios), the hard truth that fairness metrics mathematically conflict, and the mitigation toolbox across pre-, in-, and post-processing.
t_bias.exam: Know the metric names and that they can't all be satisfied at once — the governance answer is choosing metrics appropriate to context, documenting trade-offs, and testing across subgroups. 'Remove the protected attribute' is the classic wrong answer.
key_points: Bias sources: unrepresentative training data, historical discrimination encoded in labels, proxy variables, feedback loops, measurement bias
Metric menu: demographic parity (equal positive rates), equalized odds (equal error rates), equal opportunity (equal true-positive rates), predictive parity, disparate-impact ratio
Impossibility results: several fairness metrics cannot hold simultaneously except in degenerate cases — trade-offs are inherent
Mitigations: pre-processing (rebalance, reweight), in-processing (constraints during training), post-processing (threshold adjustment by group)
NIST SP 1270's three bias categories: systemic, computational/statistical, and human-cognitive — bias is not only in the data
Fairness work needs sensitive attributes for testing — governed access, not deletion, is the mature practice

t_train.overview: Getting the learning right: training data must be sufficient in volume and representative of the deployment population; overfitting (memorizing noise) and underfitting (missing signal) are the twin failure modes, managed through validation splits and regularization; labeling and ground truth quality bound everything; and the training lifecycle — including fine-tuning and retraining — carries its own risks to manage.
t_train.exam: Overfitting vs. underfitting is a guaranteed concept: overfit = excellent training scores, poor real-world performance. Representative-data scenarios (a US-trained model deployed in Asia) test the deployment-population principle.
key_points: Overfitting: model learns training noise — high train accuracy, poor generalization; regularization, more data, and early stopping counter it
Underfitting: model too simple to capture real patterns — poor everywhere; more capacity or features counter it
Representativeness beats raw volume: data must mirror the population and conditions of actual deployment
Ground truth quality caps model quality: labeling standards, inter-annotator agreement, and audit of labels matter
Fine-tuning adapts pretrained models with domain data — inheriting the base model's biases and licensing constraints
Manage risk across the training lifecycle: dataset versioning, experiment tracking, and documented retraining triggers

t_readiness.overview: The gate before production: verifying a system is production-worthy across documentation (model cards complete), legal conformity (assessments done, licenses clean), operational resilience (stress testing, failover, latency under load), adversarial robustness (red-teaming), and formal governance signoff (impact and risk reviews, go/no-go decision with named approvers).
t_readiness.exam: Checklist-style scenarios: what must be true before deployment? Strong answers combine technical readiness (stress and adversarial testing) with governance readiness (documented approvals, conformity, rollback plan) — either alone is incomplete.
key_points: Readiness evaluation spans safety, accountability, and suitability for the deployment context — not just accuracy
Stress testing: expected and edge-case workloads, latency/throughput benchmarks, resource limits, failover behavior
Red-teaming: deliberate adversarial attempts to break the system — prompts, inputs, and misuse scenarios — before attackers and users do
Legal/regulatory gate: conformity assessments, data provenance and licensing verification, insurance-driven requirements
Formal reviews with named approvers and documented go/no-go criteria — deployment is a governed decision with an audit trail
A rollback plan is part of readiness: know how to retreat before you advance

t_deployment.overview: How AI reaches users deliberately: strategy choices that manage blast radius — canary releases (small percentage first), phased rollouts (expanding cohorts with checkpoints), shadow mode (running non-authoritatively alongside the incumbent), A/B testing, blue-green switches — plus environment decisions (cloud, on-prem, edge) and the change-management work that readies people and processes.
t_deployment.exam: Vocabulary questions on the strategy names, and scenario questions choosing a strategy for a risk profile: high-stakes system → shadow mode or small canary with defined success gates before expansion.
key_points: Canary: release to a small user percentage, monitor, expand — early detection with limited impact
Phased rollout: staged expansion across users/regions/use cases with go/no-go checkpoints per phase
Shadow mode: model runs in parallel without affecting decisions — validates real-world behavior at zero user risk
A/B deployment compares variants on live traffic; blue-green keeps an instant-rollback environment warm
Deployment includes people: user training, workflow changes, communication, and support readiness (change management)
Rollback criteria defined in advance: what metric excursion or incident triggers retreat, decided before launch

t_monitoring.overview: Production vigilance: watching model performance (accuracy proxies, error patterns), data drift (input distributions shifting) and concept drift (input→output relationships shifting), fairness across groups over time, security anomalies, and usage patterns including over-reliance — with alert thresholds, escalation paths, and retraining triggers defined so detection leads to action.
t_monitoring.exam: Drift definitions are precision-tested: data drift vs. concept drift. Scenario pattern: monitoring detects degradation → investigate root cause, assess impact, remediate (possibly retrain), document — 'continue as-is' and 'immediately retrain without diagnosis' both lose.
key_points: Data drift: production inputs diverge from training distribution; concept drift: the real-world relationship the model learned has changed
Monitor multiple axes: performance, drift, fairness metrics over time, latency/availability, security signals, usage and reliance patterns
Ground-truth lag is real: proxies (confidence distributions, agreement rates, downstream outcomes) stand in when labels arrive late
Thresholds → alerts → owners → playbooks: monitoring without a response path is dashboard theater
Retraining is a governed event: triggered by defined criteria, validated like a new model, regression-tested before release
EU AI Act requires post-market monitoring for high-risk systems — this topic is a legal duty, not just hygiene

t_riskmgmt.overview: The risk discipline applied to AI: identify risks across the lifecycle, analyze likelihood and impact, evaluate against defined risk appetite and tolerance, treat (mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept), track in a register with owners, and repeat — because AI risk moves. Forecasting adds horizon-scanning for emerging risks: new attack classes, regulatory shifts, capability jumps.
t_riskmgmt.exam: Vocabulary precision: appetite (willingness) vs. tolerance (acceptable deviation), inherent vs. residual risk. Treatment-selection scenarios reward proportionate, documented choices with named owners — and 'accept' is legitimate when documented and within tolerance.
key_points: Cycle: identify → analyze (likelihood × impact) → evaluate vs. appetite → treat → monitor → repeat
Treatments: mitigate (controls), transfer (insurance/contracts), avoid (don't do it), accept (documented, within tolerance)
Risk register: each risk with owner, scores, treatment, status, and residual risk — the living record auditors ask for first
Residual risk is what remains after controls — it must be explicitly accepted by someone with authority
AI-specific registers draw from taxonomies like NIST AI RMF categories, ISO/IEC 23894 risk sources, and MITRE ATLAS threat patterns
Forecasting: horizon-scan regulation, threats, and capability shifts — yesterday's register doesn't cover tomorrow's model

t_audit.overview: Verification with independence: internal audits (independent of the AI's builders), external audits and certifications (ISO/IEC 42001 for management systems), algorithmic audits targeting bias or specific harms, and regulator-facing conformity evidence. What makes an audit real: defined criteria, qualified independent auditors, evidence-based findings, and tracked remediation.
t_audit.exam: Independence is the tested principle — the team that built the model doesn't audit it. Know the assurance stack (self-assessment < internal audit < external certification) and that audits verify against criteria (a framework, standard, or regulation), not vibes.
key_points: Audit anatomy: defined scope and criteria → independent qualified auditors → evidence collection → findings → remediation tracking → closure
Independence requirement: organizational separation from the audited system's developers and operators
Certification targets: ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management system) is the certifiable standard; NYC LL144 mandates independent bias audits for hiring tools
Algorithmic audits probe specific properties: disparate impact, robustness, privacy leakage — with quantitative evidence
Audit trails depend on earlier discipline: no logs, no lineage, no documentation → nothing to audit — governance is audit-enablement
Findings feed the risk register and corrective-action process; an unremediated finding is a standing risk acceptance

t_incident.overview: When AI goes wrong in the world: detection channels (monitoring, user reports, audits, media), containment (rollback, kill switches, scope reduction), root-cause investigation, remediation, and the disclosure matrix — EU AI Act serious-incident reports, personal-data breach notifications, sector regulators, affected individuals — followed by institutionalizing the lessons.
t_incident.exam: Lifecycle-order questions and disclosure triggers: a high-risk system's serious incident goes to market surveillance authorities; a training-data breach starts GDPR's 72-hour clock. 'Fix quietly and move on' is always the wrong answer.
key_points: Lifecycle: detect → contain → investigate root cause → remediate → disclose as required → capture lessons → update controls
Detection is multi-channel: automated monitoring, user reports, internal escalation, external researchers, media — design intake for all of them
Containment options pre-planned: rollback to prior version, disable features, constrain scope, full shutdown — with authority to invoke defined
EU AI Act: providers of high-risk systems report serious incidents to authorities (15 days standard, faster for the gravest cases)
Parallel clocks: GDPR breach notification (72 hours to DPA), sector regulators, contractual notice duties — one incident, many obligations
Root cause over blame: fixes address systemic causes (data, process, design), and post-incident reviews update the risk register

t_records.overview: The evidentiary layer of AI governance: business records proving what was decided, tested, approved, monitored, and fixed — kept per retention schedules that balance legal obligations (EU AI Act documentation retention, sector rules, litigation holds) against minimization. If governance happened but nobody documented it, auditors and regulators treat it as not having happened.
t_records.exam: Retention-tension questions (keep for accountability vs. delete for minimization → follow the documented schedule serving both) and EU AI Act specifics: high-risk providers keep technical documentation and logs — 10 years is the anchor number.
key_points: Record set: design decisions, data provenance, test results, approvals, monitoring outputs, incidents, model versions, communications
Retention schedules are policy: defined periods per record type, driven by regulation, litigation exposure, and business need
EU AI Act: high-risk providers retain technical documentation 10 years after market placement; deployers retain logs per obligations
Logs must be useful: timestamped, attributable, tamper-resistant, and retrievable — a log nobody can query is not a control
Litigation holds override routine deletion the moment litigation is reasonably anticipated
Records serve minimization too: documented deletion per schedule is defensible; ad-hoc deletion looks like spoliation

t_comms.overview: What the organization says about its AI: user-facing transparency (you are interacting with AI; this content is synthetic), public transparency reports, regulator communications, and marketing — where every capability claim must be accurate and substantiated or it becomes FTC §5 deception exposure. Crisis communication for AI incidents belongs here too.
t_comms.exam: Two reliable angles: transparency duties (EU AI Act limited-risk disclosures, deepfake labeling) and truthful-claims discipline (AI-washing scenarios). The instinct: say what the system actually does, disclose AI interactions, and prepare incident communications in advance.
key_points: EU AI Act transparency: disclose chatbot interactions, label AI-generated/deepfake content, inform about emotion-recognition or biometric categorization exposure
Marketing discipline: AI claims need substantiation before publication — capability inflation is actionable deception
Transparency reports: voluntary but increasingly expected — system purposes, safeguards, metrics, incident summaries
Regulator communications are records: accurate, consistent, and reviewed — misleading an authority has its own EU AI Act penalty tier
Incident communications planned in advance: who speaks, to whom, with what approved facts — improvised crisis messaging compounds harm

t_retire.overview: The governed end of life: retirement triggers (obsolescence, unacceptable risk, regulatory change, business exit), decommissioning plans covering dependency wind-down and successor transition, data disposition per retention and deletion obligations, stakeholder notification, and record preservation that outlives the system itself.
t_retire.exam: Checklist scenarios: what does responsible retirement require? Answers that just 'turn it off' miss data obligations, notifications, and records. Deactivation policies — predefined triggers and procedures — are the mature-practice marker.
key_points: Retirement triggers: performance decay, unacceptable risk, regulatory shifts, vendor end-of-life, strategic change — predefined in a deactivation policy
Decommissioning plan: dependency inventory, successor transition, timeline, rollback-during-retirement contingency
Data disposition: delete, return, or archive per contractual and legal obligations — including derived data and the model artifacts themselves
Notify stakeholders: users, customers, integrators, and where applicable regulators — silence creates orphaned reliance
Records survive the system: retention obligations (e.g., EU AI Act documentation) continue after decommissioning
Post-retirement verification: confirm access removal, credential revocation, and monitoring shutdown — zombie systems are unmanaged risk
